clippings.speaker: Steven Spielberg
clippings.quote: This year marks our 40th year of working together, and I have to say, without question, John Williams has been the single most significant contributor to my success as a filmmaker.
clippings.title: John Williams' Inevitable Themes
clippings.context: Spielberg's tribute at the Tanglewood gala for Williams's 80th birthday, summer 2012, as aired by NPR; Williams was then scoring Lincoln.

clippings.speaker: Steven Spielberg
clippings.quote: John is much more of a chameleon as a composer. He reinvents himself with every picture. The score to 'Tintin' could not be more dissimilar to his score to 'War Horse.'
clippings.title: John Williams and Steven Spielberg: A 40-year collaboration
clippings.context: Spielberg by phone from the Lincoln set to Rebecca Keegan, after Tintin and War Horse opened the same week in December 2011.

clippings.speaker: Steven Spielberg
clippings.quote: …you looked up at me and you were smiling, and I started laughing because I didn’t know you that well. I thought you were pulling my leg. … God knows the shark never worked, but Johnny did.
clippings.title: John Williams Startles Steven Spielberg by Telling Him He’s Not Retiring After All
clippings.context: Spielberg recalling the first piano demo of the two-note Jaws theme, onstage with Williams at an American Cinematheque conversation at the Writers Guild Theater, Jan. 12, 2023.

clippings.speaker: Steven Spielberg
clippings.quote: He said, ‘Look, unlike what we usually do, you’re not gonna come over to the office. I’m not gonna try to play this on the piano because, quite frankly, it’s impossible. Just show up at the session.’ And I got to hear it for the first time, cold.
clippings.title: John Williams Startles Steven Spielberg by Telling Him He’s Not Retiring After All
clippings.context: Spielberg on how Williams broke their usual piano-preview routine for the jazz main title of Catch Me If You Can, at the same 2023 American Cinematheque conversation.

clippings.speaker: Steven Spielberg
clippings.quote: When he first saw the picture, he talked about the nobility of these animals. We never called them monsters, we never called them dinosaurs. We called them animals.
clippings.title: A Magical Half-Century Partnership
clippings.context: Spielberg after a clip of the first dinosaur reveal in Jurassic Park, at the January 2023 American Cinematheque conversation; reported by Classical California hosts who attended.

clippings.speaker: John Williams
clippings.quote: My relationship with Steven is the result of a lot of very compatible dissimilarities. … Steven works with huge groups of people and is an international businessman. … It is a labor-intensive, solitary business.
clippings.title: John Williams and Steven Spielberg: A 40-year collaboration
clippings.context: Williams to the Los Angeles Times in his Universal lot bungalow in late December 2011, contrasting Spielberg's world with his own pencil-and-paper work.

clippings.speaker: John Williams
clippings.quote: It was like going with a teenager who had never ordered wine before and didn't quite know what to do with the silver. He was so young, a little older than my children but not a whole lot. And seemed to know more about my music than I did.
clippings.title: John Williams and Steven Spielberg: A 40-year collaboration
clippings.context: Williams recalling the 1972 lunch in Beverly Hills where the 25-year-old Spielberg recruited him for The Sugarland Express.

clippings.speaker: John Williams
clippings.quote: He’s always been a positive collaborator. He’s never anything but appreciative of me. … When we record, he has almost physical pleasure from what the orchestra is playing, all the time.
clippings.title: Q&A: John Williams on accompanying Steven Spielberg
clippings.context: Phone Q&A before a 2013 Phoenix Symphony benefit concert with both men; Williams answering a question about Spielberg thinking the Jaws theme was a joke.

clippings.speaker: John Williams
clippings.quote: The lights went up and the film was over, and I couldn’t breathe. … I said: ‘Steven, this is a great, great film. And you need a better composer than I am to do this score.’ And he said, ‘I know…but they’re all dead!’
clippings.title: A Magical Half-Century Partnership
clippings.context: Williams recounting his first screening of Schindler's List (1993), at the January 2023 American Cinematheque conversation.

clippings.speaker: John Williams
clippings.quote: Why have Steven and I stayed together for 50 years? What held us together was the fact that I loved this man immediately, when he was a baby. … In a way, I was kind of looking in the same direction that Steven was always in our love for fulfillment and our desire to measure up to the shoulders we stood on.
clippings.title: John Williams Startles Steven Spielberg by Telling Him He’s Not Retiring After All
clippings.context: Williams summing up their 50-year partnership and shared love of Golden Age Hollywood composers (Korngold, Waxman, Steiner) at the 2023 American Cinematheque conversation.

clippings.speaker: Martin Scorsese
clippings.quote: So Thelma finally decided to put this long tracking shot of Bill up there.
clippings.title: Thelma Schoonmaker & Martin Scorsese on 'Gangs of New York'
clippings.context: Joint Q&A with Norm Hollyn for the Editors Guild magazine; Scorsese explains how Thelma reshaped the opening Five Points sequence.

clippings.speaker: Martin Scorsese
clippings.quote: For me the editing process of a film is my favourite and a lot of it has to do with the time I spend working with Thelma together. We live through every film together and every film is a whole lifetime in and of itself…
clippings.title: Martin Scorsese's editor Thelma Schoonmaker honoured with Bafta Fellowship
clippings.context: From Scorsese's video tribute played before Thelma accepted the BAFTA Fellowship at the Royal Albert Hall; reported in a PA wire story.

clippings.speaker: Thelma Schoonmaker
clippings.quote: I want to thank, first of all, Marty Scorsese; he edited this film with me every minute of the time.
clippings.title: Thelma Schoonmaker Academy Awards Acceptance Speech (Film Editing, Raging Bull)
clippings.context: Official transcript of her first Oscar acceptance speech, at the 53rd Academy Awards.

clippings.speaker: Thelma Schoonmaker
clippings.quote: Money didn’t mean anything to me, but working with people who cared as deeply as someone like Marty did about their films is very seductive — you never want to work any other way.
clippings.title: His Girl Friday: Thelma Schoonmaker Cuts Things Down to Size
clippings.context: Terrence Rafferty's 1982 profile, written while she and Scorsese were cutting The King of Comedy (republished in the Voice archives, 2018).

clippings.speaker: Thelma Schoonmaker
clippings.quote: This is really as much yours as it is mine, Marty, not only because you helped me edit the movie, but because you think like an editor when you shoot.
clippings.title: Thelma Schoonmaker Academy Awards Acceptance Speech (Film Editing, The Aviator)
clippings.context: Official transcript of her second Oscar acceptance speech, at the 77th Academy Awards; she closes with "But it's really you, Marty. It's you."

clippings.speaker: Thelma Schoonmaker
clippings.quote: We work very compatibly. We're very different. I'm very optimistic and calm and patient, and Marty is emotional and dramatic. We balance each other.
clippings.title: Thelma Schoonmaker, Scorsese's Favorite Editor
clippings.context: Transcript of her 2005 interview with Terry Gross, answering what the give and take is like in the editing room.

clippings.speaker: Thelma Schoonmaker
clippings.quote: Working with Marty is quite something. It's tumultuous, passionate, funny and it's like being in the best film school in the world.
clippings.title: Thelma Schoonmaker Academy Awards Acceptance Speech (Film Editing, The Departed)
clippings.context: Official transcript of her third Oscar acceptance speech, at the 79th Academy Awards.

clippings.speaker: Thelma Schoonmaker
clippings.quote: And he's a great editor, Marty. It's his favorite part of filmmaking. So that was very hard,
clippings.title: Thelma Schoonmaker Reflects On "Silence," Editing For Scorsese and Powell
clippings.context: AP interview by Jake Coyle in the office where they cut Silence; she continues: "I think he sensed with me that we could collaborate and it wouldn't be an ego fight all the time."

clippings.speaker: Thelma Schoonmaker
clippings.quote: Marty introduced me to Michael Powell not expecting we would fall in love and marry, but we did, and this gave me the happiest 10 years of my life.
clippings.title: Martin Scorsese's editor Thelma Schoonmaker honoured with Bafta Fellowship
clippings.context: From her BAFTA Fellowship acceptance speech, the same night as Scorsese's video tribute.

clippings.speaker: Ennio Morricone
clippings.quote: We went to primary school together but only for a year and I can’t say we were great friends. It was only later on, when he asked me to do the music for Fistful of Dollars, that our friendship developed.
clippings.title: “If you want to call yourself a composer, you follow every step of the instrumentation:” Ennio Morricone interviewed in 2006
clippings.context: Telephone interview with Guido Bonsaver, first published in Sight and Sound's July 2006 issue and reposted by the BFI in 2023; asked whether he and Leone had known each other since childhood.

clippings.speaker: Ennio Morricone
clippings.quote: That was his invention, though I remember I had talked to him about an experiment in Florence where musicians had theorised that any sound or noise taken out of context and totally isolated would acquire a new meaning. His idea of the 20-minute sequence based on the waterdrop was, I think, inspired by that conversation.
clippings.film: Once Upon a Time in the West
clippings.title: “If you want to call yourself a composer, you follow every step of the instrumentation:” Ennio Morricone interviewed in 2006
clippings.context: Same 2006 Sight and Sound interview; asked about the music-free opening sequence (water dripping on Woody Strode's hat).

clippings.speaker: Ennio Morricone
clippings.quote: Leone's films were made like that because he wanted the music to be an important part of it, and he often kept the scenes longer simply because he didn't want the music to end. That's why the films were so slow - because they were following the pattern of the music.
clippings.title: 'A Fistful of Dollars? It's my worst ever score'
clippings.context: Interview with Will Hodgkinson, translated through an interpreter; Morricone first snapped "Who told him not to ask me about Leone?" before explaining why he wrote some music before the films were shot.

clippings.speaker: Ennio Morricone
clippings.quote: Leone allowed lots of space for music, that was his personal style, and it ended up being a very intense collaboration. I would initially play him the music on piano, which didn't give much idea of how it would eventually sound – he was often shocked. But pleasantly shocked I think.
clippings.title: Ennio Morricone 1928-2020: A lost afternoon in his apartment in Rome
clippings.context: Peter Culshaw's 2003 interview in Morricone's Rome apartment, through a translator, republished after his death.

clippings.speaker: Ennio Morricone
clippings.quote: There is a lot of talking, of listening to things. Quite frequently, everything is scrapped and we start again from scratch. Often when everything has been accepted Sergio starts to doubt the decision and then more doubts come.
clippings.film: Once Upon a Time in America
clippings.title: Ennio Morricone: Interview (1984)
clippings.context: Answer to Sue Adler's question "What is your working relationship with Sergio Leone?" in Cinema Papers, December 1984, the year Once Upon a Time in America came out; full interview reprinted online.

clippings.speaker: Ennio Morricone
clippings.quote: It stems primarily from Leone’s style, which allowed more time, more space, for music than that of other directors. It wasn’t because of our friendship; it was strictly his particular style.
clippings.title: An Interview with Ennio Morricone (1994)
clippings.context: 1994 interview with Jon Burlingame and Gary Crowdus with simultaneous translation, published in Cineaste Vol. 21 No. 1/2 (1995) and reprinted online; asked whether European directors give music more room.

clippings.speaker: Ennio Morricone
clippings.quote: I missed a great opportunity and I am really sorry. When Clint called me, I said no out of respect to Sergio Leone, not because I did not like the movies that he did.
clippings.title: Why A Western Icon Regretted Turning Down The Opportunity To Work With Clint Eastwood
clippings.context: Morricone telling the BBC in 2014 why he turned down Clint Eastwood's films after Leone and Eastwood fell out; quoted by /Film because the BBC original could not be fetched.

clippings.speaker: Sergio Leone
clippings.quote: I’ve always felt that music is more expressive than dialogue. I’ve always said that my best dialogue and screenwriter is Ennio Morricone. Because, many times, it is more important a note or an orchestration than a line said.
clippings.title: An Interview with Sergio Leone (1987)
clippings.context: Marlaine Glicksman's interview at Leone's home outside Rome in September 1987, translated live by actor Brian Freilino; first published online in 2012 by ASX with the interviewer's rights.

clippings.speaker: Sergio Leone
clippings.quote: From Ennio I ask for themes that clothe my characters easily. He’s never read a script of mine to compose the music, because many times he’s composed the music before the script is ever written.
clippings.title: An Interview with Sergio Leone (1987)
clippings.context: Same 1987 Glicksman interview, translated live; answer to "Ennio Morricone writes the music to your films before you shoot them."

clippings.speaker: Sergio Leone
clippings.quote: ‘Well, sorry, it’s just that this music seems crap to me – just as it did four months ago. You told me that everything would be different with the arrangement but nothing has changed!’ … Immediately I ask him: ‘Have you seen Walt Disney’s Lady and the Tramp?’ ‘Yes,’ he replies, ‘but what has that got to do with Cheyenne?’
clippings.film: Once Upon a Time in the West
clippings.publication: Christopher Frayling, Something to Do with Death
clippings.title: Ennio Morricone and the Scoring of “Once Upon a Time in the West”
clippings.context: Leone recalling how the Cheyenne theme was saved at the recording session, as quoted in Frayling's 2000 biography (translated) and reposted online; the original interview isn't named.

clippings.speaker: Christopher Nolan
clippings.quote: I wrote out a page of what I considered to be the heart of the story—the relationships, the idea of a father having to leave his children … I gave it to Hans and said, ‘Work on that for a day and give me what you’ve got at the end of the day, and that’ll be the seed from which we can grow the score.’
clippings.title: The Iris Interview: Christopher Nolan, Jonathan Nolan and Emma Thomas talk about working on Interstellar
clippings.context: Nolan's own account of the one-page letter he gave Zimmer before writing the script, in a Q&A with Jonathan Nolan and Emma Thomas.

clippings.speaker: Hans Zimmer
clippings.quote: I played him this thing, and it’s tiny, a musical love letter to my son. And I said to him, ‘What do you think?’ And he paused for a second, and said, ‘I’d better make the movie now.’
clippings.title: OscarWrap: Christopher Nolan and ‘Interstellar’ Dream Team Talk Sound, Edit, Design
clippings.context: Zimmer, interviewed by Steve Pond for TheWrap's awards issue, describes playing Nolan the piece he wrote in a day from the one-page letter.

clippings.speaker: Hans Zimmer
clippings.quote: Well it’s really simple. The answer is Chris Nolan and the way we work together. We get breathless with throwing ideas at each other and we cross all the lines. It’s like Chris will be talking about music and I’ll be talking about story.
clippings.title: Hans Zimmer Talks About Scoring Interstellar, and Why Batman Needs a New Theme
clippings.context: Interview with Don Kaye; Zimmer answering why he writes such good scores for Nolan, right after describing Nolan as 'part of the band' in his studio.

clippings.speaker: Christopher Nolan
clippings.quote: What I decided to do was give it to Hans and let him run with it and see if in some way it might inform elements of the score
clippings.title: INCEPTION Interview Leonardo DiCaprio, Joseph Gordon-Levitt, Ellen Page, Marion Cotillard, Tom Hardy, Ken Watanabe, Christopher Nolan, Hans Zimmer
clippings.context: Inception press conference transcript; Nolan on handing Zimmer the Edith Piaf song from the script so it could shape the score.

clippings.speaker: Hans Zimmer
clippings.quote: In a funny way, what I think we did do was a sort of shared dreaming thing, and we did prove it’s possible, because when I finally saw the film, and when Chris had laid in all my music, I was actually surprised how well these two worlds existed together.
clippings.title: INCEPTION Interview Leonardo DiCaprio, Joseph Gordon-Levitt, Ellen Page, Marion Cotillard, Tom Hardy, Ken Watanabe, Christopher Nolan, Hans Zimmer
clippings.context: Same press conference; Zimmer explains that Nolan would not show him footage until he had written the music.

clippings.speaker: Christopher Nolan
clippings.quote: I asked Hans not to write any emotional music. What I said to him was I wanted objectivity — the way I wanted to make the film was, it’s all about suspense and tension and not at all about emotion.
clippings.title: ‘Dunkirk’ soundtrack: How it all came together
clippings.context: Melena Ryzik's New York Times piece on the Dunkirk score (July 2017), syndicated openly by Gulf News; Nolan spoke separately from Vietnam during the press tour.

clippings.speaker: Christopher Nolan
clippings.quote: I didn’t really say this to Hans, but it played at my father’s funeral a few years ago. I just find it unbearably moving.
clippings.title: ‘Dunkirk’ soundtrack: How it all came together
clippings.context: Nolan on why he suggested Elgar's 'Nimrod' for the Dunkirk score, which Zimmer then slowed and reworked.

clippings.speaker: Hans Zimmer
clippings.quote: This was the closest collaboration that I ever had with a director where even though he would never ever play a note, he somehow played every note that was in that score.
clippings.title: ‘Dunkirk’ soundtrack: How it all came together
clippings.context: Zimmer to the New York Times on Dunkirk; in the same piece he adds, 'Can I say something rude? This score is Chris Nolan’s score.'

clippings.speaker: Hans Zimmer
clippings.quote: Chris [Nolan] understands I have to do it. He’s going to be just fine. Ludwig and I are friends. Forget the friend part, he’s really good.
clippings.title: Here’s why Hans Zimmer isn’t working on Christopher Nolan’s next film
clippings.context: Zimmer explaining why he chose Dune over Tenet, which went to Ludwig Göransson; originally said on The Playlist's podcast, which Yahoo does not credit by name.

clippings.speaker: Hans Zimmer
clippings.quote: Not great. … So Chris realized that, and he realized that that’s where my focus was at that moment.
clippings.title: How Christopher Nolan Reacted to Hans Zimmer Choosing Dune Over Tenet
clippings.context: Zimmer on CinemaBlend's ReelBlend podcast, asked how Nolan took the news; the elided middle explains that touring had pulled his focus toward Dune.

clippings.speaker: Denis Villeneuve
clippings.quote: A privilege. It was the first time in my life that I had the opportunity to work with a master; someone who is in control of his art, and someone who had the generosity to share it with me. I felt, all the time, that Roger wanted to serve my vision and to protect my identity as a filmmaker.
clippings.title: Interview with Denis Villeneuve for PRISONERS
clippings.context: Asked what it was like to work with Deakins, in a press interview for Prisoners, their first film together.

clippings.speaker: Roger Deakins
clippings.quote: I heard Denis was doing this movie and got the script, which was dense and had a lot of characters, and, to be honest, Gothic elements that I thought went too far. I wasn’t interested in that genre, but it turned out that Denis wasn’t, either.
clippings.title: Beyond the Law: Prisoners
clippings.context: Deakins on signing on to Prisoners after admiring Incendies, in American Cinematographer's Prisoners story by David E. Williams (republished on theasc.com).

clippings.speaker: Roger Deakins
clippings.quote: Denis is incredibly good with actors and working through a scene and finding something that’s not just there on the page. I thought that was really intense, really interesting. When he found something, he knows if he wants it or not. He’s very decisive like that. But he’s also very meticulous with the camera.
clippings.title: Famed Cinematographer Roger Deakins Talks Coens, Storytelling, ‘Prisoners’
clippings.context: Anne Thompson asked Deakins, via Skype from the Unbroken shoot, whether Villeneuve is a precise director.

clippings.speaker: Denis Villeneuve
clippings.quote: It’s pretty rare for me, but at the beginning, I must say I was a little intimidated by Roger. So we had to learn to work together on Prisoners. And then I wanted to pursue our relationship, and go further visually. Sicario was a film I really had to make with Roger; I needed someone with his mastery of the frame and space, and I wanted to go into the night with him.
clippings.title: Sicario: Interview with Denis Villeneuve
clippings.context: Benjamin B's extended interview for the ASC's The Film Book blog, companion to his October 2015 American Cinematographer article on Sicario.

clippings.speaker: Denis Villeneuve
clippings.quote: For example, one time on ‘Sicario’ we were working with a 32 mm lens, and I said, ‘Roger, I think we should go with a longer lens. I feel that the image lacks rhythm right now. It should be much more compressed.’ And Roger said, ‘You’re totally right.’ Then he called out to his camera assistant, ‘Bring me a 35mm lens!’ I was expecting an 85 or 100 mm lens. I was laughing so much. With Roger, every millimeter has a strong effect and meaning.
clippings.title: Denis Villeneuve on working with Roger Deakins
clippings.context: Told to Jon Fauer at Cannes, at the reception before Deakins received the Pierre Angénieux Excellens Award, the weekend Sicario premiered there.

clippings.speaker: Roger Deakins
clippings.quote: We compliment each other quite well, it’s chemistry. You get on with some people better than you get on with others. We’ve certainly had a similar take on the two films and we share similar ideas.
clippings.title: FPH Interview: Roger Deakins
clippings.context: Phone interview with Michael Bergeron during Sicario's release, after Prisoners and before Blade Runner 2049.

clippings.speaker: Roger Deakins
clippings.quote: No! We bandy things around. He’s very sweet, but it really is a collaboration. We go back and forth. With anybody I’ll say my opinion: I don’t think I’m there just to keep mum and push a button.
clippings.title: 'If the Camera Moves it’s Got To Be for a Reason': An Interview with Roger Deakins
clippings.context: At TIFF, Calum Marsh said Villeneuve had seemed deferential to Deakins when talking about him; this is Deakins' reply.

clippings.speaker: Denis Villeneuve
clippings.quote: The thing is that I need to say that I brought Roger on board day one. I said yes in the morning I met him at the dinner at his home at night, and I asked him right away, ’Will you join me?’ and he said, ’Yes’ with a smile right away. I knew he was dreaming to do science-fiction, to go back to science-fiction, and he was very excited right from the start.
clippings.title: 'Blade Runner 2049' Director Denis Villeneuve On Building The Future And Taking Ridley Scott's Advice [Interview]
clippings.context: Villeneuve on recruiting Deakins the same day he agreed to direct Blade Runner 2049.

clippings.speaker: Roger Deakins
clippings.quote: I love science fiction, but you’ve got to have a good story, and I wanted to make this movie because I thought the script was pretty damn good, and I wanted to work with Denis again.
clippings.title: Uncanny Valley
clippings.context: Deakins on why he took Blade Runner 2049, in Rachael K. Bosley's December 2017 American Cinematographer cover story (PDF).

clippings.speaker: Denis Villeneuve
clippings.quote: I'm in a learning process working with you. It's very rewarding and exciting. Right now I am doing VFX on 'Dune,' and I found myself talking about light and asking for things and I'm like, 'I know it's Roger.' I know that I can do things [because of Roger].
clippings.title: Villeneuve Isn’t Ready to Rewatch ‘Blade Runner 2049,’ Says Deakins Influenced ‘Dune’
clippings.context: Said to Deakins on the Team Deakins podcast (July 2020), as quoted by IndieWire's Zack Sharf; Deakins did not shoot Dune (Greig Fraser did).

clippings.speaker: Robert De Niro
clippings.quote: I forgot my lines so the director wrote them down for me. … And Marty Scorsese, who gave me and all the other actors and everyone on the film all the love and trust that anyone could give anyone and is just wonderful as a director.
clippings.title: Robert De Niro, Actor in a Leading Role, Raging Bull (53rd Academy Awards)
clippings.context: Best Actor acceptance speech for Raging Bull at the 53rd Academy Awards, read from notes.

clippings.speaker: Robert De Niro
clippings.quote: You still have the same passion, drive and intensity you had when we were starting out together. As for me? Well, I'm doing comedy. … But don't worry, Marty, I still have enough misery in me for us to do a few more pictures together.
clippings.title: The 30th Annual Kennedy Center Honors (CBS press release)
clippings.context: De Niro's onstage tribute when Scorsese was a Kennedy Center honoree, Dec. 2, 2007, as transcribed in CBS's broadcast press release.

clippings.speaker: Robert De Niro
clippings.quote: Marty knows so many movies. If I have a question about any film I'm trying to find, I always ask him, of course, and he will know. There's no comparison. I wish I knew the movies as much as he does. We'll talk about some obscure film or he'll tell me about it and then send me a bunch of films of this director from Africa. I mean, God bless him. I don't watch as much as I should.
clippings.title: Irishman Week: Robert De Niro interview
clippings.context: Asked whether he tries to keep up with Scorsese's film viewing, in an April 2019 interview at De Niro's Tribeca office.

clippings.speaker: Robert De Niro
clippings.quote: How could I not relate to that? … Me and Marty both. You get older, and what's it all about, Alfie? That's it. … I don't know where we're gonna be in 10 years, in 15 years. … But with Marty, I will always say yes.
clippings.title: Robert De Niro Lets Us In On the Secret of Creating Film's Greatest Collaboration With Scorsese
clippings.context: Interview with Eric Kohn during The Irishman press tour, on the film's meditation on aging and whether their next film would be their last.

clippings.speaker: Robert De Niro
clippings.quote: The thought was unthinkable to me to move on without Marty. But I had to give him that out and ask him if he wanted to do it. … I do recall telling him he could really make this picture special and we would have something that would be remembered for all the right reasons. To me, there was nobody else who could do it better – period.
clippings.title: Raging Bull book reveals Robert De Niro saved 'near death' Martin Scorsese's life in late-1970s
clippings.context: De Niro recalling his 1978 hospital visit to Scorsese, as told to author Jay Glennie for the book Raging Bull: The Making Of and quoted by The Independent.

clippings.speaker: Robert De Niro
clippings.quote: Marty is... very easy about stuff, listens, lets you do what you want and if it's wrong - not even wrong - he suggests another way of doing it... Our experience has been special in that we've been able to go all these years and come up with stuff. Sometimes I come up with stuff, sometimes it's ideas Marty has.
clippings.title: Robert De Niro and Martin Scorsese on why Raging Bull almost didn't happen
clippings.context: Pretaped Tribeca Festival 2021 closing-night conversation about Raging Bull, moderated by Leonardo DiCaprio.

clippings.speaker: Martin Scorsese
clippings.quote: We learned to make movies together, and what we learned you can see in every picture I've made ever since.
clippings.title: De Niro Honored As "The Gold Standard"
clippings.context: Scorsese's tribute when De Niro was a Kennedy Center honoree in December 2009, as reported by CBS.

clippings.speaker: Martin Scorsese
clippings.quote: He got what I was trying to do in that picture. … As we kept working together and became close friends, a kind of artistic partnership came into being. It had to do with our shared experience, building from that, but always exploring new territory, always wanting to surprise ourselves, to discover values and colors that we'd never envisioned.
clippings.title: Robert De Niro Lets Us In On the Secret of Creating Film's Greatest Collaboration With Scorsese
clippings.context: Scorsese, via email to IndieWire, on De Niro in Mean Streets and how their partnership grew from it.

clippings.speaker: Martin Scorsese
clippings.quote: Now I knew what he had in mind, Bob, because when he presented the idea to me – and I hadn't read the book yet – he became rather emotional, and I realised that's the key. If I could feel the same way, or create something that allows me to get to that emotional state, creatively, that might be the way to go.
clippings.title: Martin Scorsese on The Irishman: the Sight & Sound Interview
clippings.context: Interview with Philip Horne, on De Niro bringing him Charles Brandt's book I Heard You Paint Houses.

clippings.speaker: Martin Scorsese
clippings.quote: Right before, we'd done Taxi Driver, so I was interested in anything he'd present to me, but... I wasn't affected by the book at all.
clippings.title: Robert De Niro and Martin Scorsese on why Raging Bull almost didn't happen
clippings.context: Tribeca Festival 2021 conversation, on his initial reaction when De Niro brought him Jake LaMotta's memoir.

clippings.speaker: Martin Scorsese
clippings.quote: He wanted me to do Analyze This, and I said, ‘We already did it. It was Goodfellas.’ I talked to him about other projects, and at one point he said, ‘You know the kind of stuff I like to do with you.’ I said, ‘OK.’ That became The Irishman, and it took nine years. We were always looking. ‘What about The Departed?’ ‘Nah, I don't wanna do that.’ ‘OK.’
clippings.title: Martin Scorsese, Leonardo DiCaprio & Robert De Niro On How They Found The Emotional Handle For Their Cannes Epic 'Killers Of The Flower Moon': The Deadline Q&A
clippings.context: Same Cannes Q&A, on the projects they offered each other and turned down in the years between Casino and The Irishman.

clippings.speaker: Martin Scorsese
clippings.quote: he is the only one around who knows where I came from and who I am, from that period of time when we were 15 or 16 years old. He knows that part of New York. It was all instinct between us and his courage and his humility, in terms of how he'll say, ‘If a scene plays on my back, fine, but if it plays better on the other person's face, play that.’
clippings.title: Martin Scorsese, Leonardo DiCaprio & Robert De Niro On How They Found The Emotional Handle For Their Cannes Epic 'Killers Of The Flower Moon': The Deadline Q&A
clippings.context: Same Cannes Q&A, on why they kept checking in with each other over the years.

clippings.speaker: Sam Raimi
clippings.quote: He’s like my long-lost brother, partner, most constant collaborator, friend. We communicate so well. He’s my actor in these movies. He’s the guy that understands me more than anybody. He’s a real problem solver, and I find him to be a brilliant comedian and somebody that will do anything to be professional and make a movie as best it can be.
clippings.film: Doctor Strange in the Multiverse of Madness
clippings.title: Q&A: Sam Raimi on ‘Doctor Strange’ and his superhero return
clippings.context: AP's Jake Coyle asked Raimi, the morning after the Multiverse of Madness premiere, how he would describe his bond with Campbell.

clippings.speaker: Sam Raimi
clippings.quote: Absolutely. I call Bruce and I say, ‘Hey baby.’ And he says, ‘What is it now?’ And I say, ‘I got another movie for you now.’ And he says, ‘When does it start?’
clippings.film: Doctor Strange in the Multiverse of Madness
clippings.title: Q&A: Sam Raimi on ‘Doctor Strange’ and his superhero return
clippings.context: Answering whether phoning Campbell is an automatic call whenever he has a film, in the same AP interview.

clippings.speaker: Sam Raimi
clippings.quote: I think it was when I was in 10th grade and met Bruce Campbell and my buddies Scott Spiegel and Tim Quill, who were all making these Super 8 movies. And it was like, ‘Oh, my gosh, these guys get together every weekend. They’ve got partners. Somebody can film. Somebody can throw the pie. Somebody can take the pie in the face. This is everything we need.’
clippings.title: Sam Raimi: The Ultimate 'Multiverse of Madness' Interview
clippings.context: Asked by Brian Hiatt when he realized he wanted to be a filmmaker professionally.

clippings.speaker: Sam Raimi
clippings.quote: Yes, Bruce has always had a lot of input, in the Evil Dead movies and now. … But most of Bruce’s input is on set. He comes up with a funny bit, or he finds a way to change a line – shorten it and get the same point across. He’s a very efficient actor and good at contributing with good ideas.
clippings.title: Exclusive: Sam Raimi Talks Ash vs. Evil Dead and Working with Bruce Campbell Again
clippings.context: Asked whether Campbell had input on the series he co-wrote with his brother Ivan, ahead of the Ash vs Evil Dead premiere.

clippings.speaker: Sam Raimi
clippings.quote: I didn’t like doing it because my favorite part of Evil Dead is working with Bruce and writing for Bruce and following his story. … My favorite part is him.
clippings.title: Ash vs. Evil Dead – Exclusive Chat with Sam Raimi and Bruce Campbell
clippings.context: Raimi explaining his reluctance to give pilot time to a new character (Lucy Lawless's Ruby) instead of Campbell's Ash.

clippings.speaker: Bruce Campbell
clippings.quote: I’d go to, you know, answer a question. He’s sitting behind me. He’ll take his pencil, put it in the back of my neck, and start to increase the pressure during the course of my answer to see how long I could last without cracking. … We had that punishment relationship right from the start.
clippings.title: TRANSCRIPT Bullseye with Jesse Thorn: Bruce Campbell
clippings.context: Campbell recalling the high-school radio speech class where the friendship began, in a 2011 interview with Jordan Morris (transcript posted with a 2025 rebroadcast).

clippings.speaker: Bruce Campbell
clippings.quote: But once we get into scenes one-on-one, it’s always the same. Sam pokes me with a stick, and you know, we have a good time. And he makes fun of me in front of the crew, and I let him do it, ’cause it makes him seem like he’s a little, you know, Rasputin character.
clippings.title: TRANSCRIPT Bullseye with Jesse Thorn: Bruce Campbell
clippings.context: On going from their Super 8 days to Raimi's 1,200-extra Spider-Man set for his wrestling-announcer cameo, same 2011 interview.

clippings.speaker: Bruce Campbell
clippings.quote: This is Sam's way of tormenting me even when he's not physically tormenting me. He's tormenting me mentally because now he knows I'm going to read in every review - the aging lothario starts by hooking up a geezer girdle and looking for his teeth.
clippings.title: Join Ussss ... Join Ussss ... For The Return Of 'Evil Dead'
clippings.context: Weekend Edition Saturday piece by Eric Deggans; Campbell on the Ash vs Evil Dead opening, in which Ash squeezes into a corset.

clippings.speaker: Bruce Campbell
clippings.quote: Sam loves to trash talk, and he loves to make fun of me in front of the crew. That's just his form of affection. He started to insult Tobey Maguire on Spider-Man, and I said, 'That's good, Tobey. That means he likes you!'
clippings.title: 'Evil Dead' star Bruce Campbell shares behind-the-scenes secrets from his 'no holds barred' horror classic
clippings.context: Ethan Alter interview for The Evil Dead's 40th anniversary; Campbell on how his Spider-Man cameos mirror their real dynamic.

clippings.speaker: Bruce Campbell
clippings.quote: Sam, he's a technically literate director. Like he read the American Cinematographers Manual. And nobody reads that crap. … Sam would learn 100% of what that camera can do, and he would make it roll over and bark.
clippings.title: Bruce Campbell Talks Sam Raimi, Evil Dead and Pizza Poppa's Backstory
clippings.context: Asked what has stayed the same in Raimi's process after decades together; he goes on to describe a punishing Army of Darkness shot.

clippings.speaker: David Fincher
clippings.quote: I called him for The Social Network because I had been listening to Ghosts I-IV. … one needle drop we had used from Ghosts—he would look at it and go, ‘Yeah, that blows, I don’t want to use it.’ We’d say, ‘Wait, we really like it’ and he’d go, ‘No, no, you’re going to like this.’ Then you’d get something and go, ‘Wow, that’s even better. He’s right.’
clippings.title: The Way Out Is Through: An Interview with David Fincher
clippings.context: Fincher, in a FADER Q&A devoted to Reznor, on why he recruited him for The Social Network after temping the film with NIN's Ghosts I-IV.

clippings.speaker: David Fincher
clippings.quote: There were times when I’d say, ‘This feels too sinister here.’ And he’d say ‘Wow, really? I thought that was a love theme.’ You don’t want your thing to be like everybody else’s, so you go to someone like Trent and say, ‘Let me try to get inside your head, you try to get inside mine, and let’s talk.’
clippings.title: The Way Out Is Through: An Interview with David Fincher
clippings.context: Fincher describing how disagreements over cues play out in their collaboration.

clippings.speaker: David Fincher
clippings.quote: He makes you better. He makes you say what you mean. He makes you ask questions. He can embarrass you, because he’ll go, ‘Well, don’t you think if she’s saying this on page three and then we have this on page 94, aren’t those two ideas connected?’ And you go, Fuck, of course they are. Above and beyond all the great music he’s made for me, I appreciate him for being somebody who’s seeing clearer and better.
clippings.title: The Way Out Is Through: An Interview with David Fincher
clippings.context: Fincher answering what's fun about solving problems with Reznor.

clippings.speaker: David Fincher
clippings.quote: Hand Covers Bruise does more for the setup of who Zuckerberg is than almost anything else in the movie … It comes to personify him. Music is about more than just supporting an idea. What Trent and Atticus do is give us a good healthy vein to get into a stranger’s operating system.
clippings.title: David Fincher and Trent Reznor on Mank: 'People were like: Huh. This is very niche'
clippings.context: Joint Zoom interview with Ryan Gilbey during the Mank Oscar campaign; Fincher looking back on The Social Network's main theme.

clippings.speaker: Trent Reznor
clippings.quote: So I told David, look, I don't think I can do - in fact, I can't do it right now. … It was nagging me that I felt I disappointed him. And I got in touch with him just to say: Listen, sorry again, and in the future, just - if anything else ever comes up, let me know. And he said: Well, I'm still waiting on you to say yes to this film.
clippings.title: Trent Reznor: Iconoclast To Icon, Via Oscar
clippings.context: Reznor to NPR's Guy Raz, weeks after the Oscar win, on initially turning Fincher down.

clippings.speaker: Trent Reznor
clippings.quote: When we finished work on ’The Social Network’ we were very proud of our work and happy to just be involved in this film, and to be standing up here in this company is humbling and flattering beyond words. … And David Fincher... David Fincher, thank you so much for the opportunity.
clippings.title: Academy Awards Acceptance Speech: Music (Original Score), The Social Network
clippings.context: Reznor's acceptance speech for Best Original Score (shared with Atticus Ross) at the 83rd Academy Awards.

clippings.speaker: Trent Reznor
clippings.quote: What we intended to do was to send David 10 to 20 rough drafts of things. I thought that would be the first of several times that we’d be doing that … Much to our surprise, we got back, ‘I think the lion’s share of composition has been done, because this works perfectly.’
clippings.title: Trent Reznor: Breaking the ‘Soundtrack’ Rules for ‘The Social Network’
clippings.context: Reznor (interviewed with Atticus Ross) on Fincher's response to their first batch of sketches.

clippings.speaker: Trent Reznor
clippings.quote: That was David coming to me and saying, ‘What do you think about a version of this?’ I wouldn’t have thought of it. … When you see it … it’s like, ‘Oh, now I get it!’ What we’ve learned is that he has a vision, and we should trust him.
clippings.film: The Girl with the Dragon Tattoo
clippings.title: NIN frontman enjoys gigs in film
clippings.context: Todd Martens' LA Times feature (syndicated by the Spokesman-Review on 2011-12-30); Reznor on Fincher's idea to cover Led Zeppelin's "Immigrant Song" with Karen O for the opening titles.

clippings.speaker: Trent Reznor
clippings.quote: [Fincher] said, 'Think about the really terrible music you hear in massage parlors. The way that it artificially tries to make you feel like everything's OK. And then imagine that sound starting to curdle and unravel.'
clippings.title: Trent Reznor Says Gone Girl Score Inspired By Terrible Music In Massage Parlors
clippings.context: Stereogum quoting a (paywalled) Wall Street Journal interview; in the same piece Fincher retorts, "I said a spa, not a massage parlor!"

clippings.speaker: Trent Reznor
clippings.quote: I remember everyone was jealous at the situation we’d walked into: the freedom granted by David, no interference, no producers weighing in, no preview audiences voting, none of that bullshit. You’re just doing the best work you can, and you’re making art.
clippings.title: David Fincher and Trent Reznor on Mank: 'People were like: Huh. This is very niche'
clippings.context: Reznor, in the joint Guardian interview, recalling awards-season roundtables after The Social Network; he contrasts it with other films, adding "That's never the case with David."

clippings.speaker: Trent Reznor
clippings.quote: David said he was thinking the film could be like something that was found in the vault, made in the same period as Citizen Kane … We thought we’d start in that world and see where it took us. What happened, to our surprise, was that it felt wildly exciting.
clippings.title: David Fincher and Trent Reznor on Mank: 'People were like: Huh. This is very niche'
clippings.context: Reznor on how Fincher's brief led to Mank's period-specific instrumentation.

clippings.speaker: Alfred Hitchcock
clippings.quote: I certainly do. … I don’t know. As far as I’m concerned he does as he likes.
clippings.title: Telescope: A Talk with Hitchcock
clippings.context: CBC's Telescope (1964, filmed at Universal during Marnie): asked by host Fletcher Markle whether he thinks highly of Herrmann's work and how they decide on music; transcript by Alan Andres for the Bernard Herrmann Society (2000).

clippings.speaker: Bernard Herrmann
clippings.quote: I’m brought in at the very beginning of the idea of a film. And by the time it has gone through all its stages of being written and rewritten and the final process of photographing it, I am so much a part of the whole thing that we have all begun to think one way.
clippings.title: Telescope: A Talk with Hitchcock
clippings.context: Herrmann, appearing on the same 1964 CBC Telescope profile of Hitchcock, describes how he works on Hitchcock's films.

clippings.speaker: Bernard Herrmann
clippings.quote: Originally the plan was in our discussions not to have any music over any of the murder scenes. However I differed with Hitch about this and I felt that music was needed. … And he said immediately [after seeing the scored version], ‘We must have the music, of course!’ And I said, ‘But you were against it.’ And he said, ‘Oh, no. All I made was an poor suggestion.’
clippings.title: Telescope: A Talk with Hitchcock
clippings.context: Herrmann on CBC Telescope (1964), with Hitchcock in the same program, telling how he scored the Psycho murders against Hitchcock's plan; the bracketed words are the transcriber's.

clippings.speaker: Bernard Herrmann
clippings.quote: Hitch has his own world of film. He’s created characters and places and stories for it very much the way Dickens did.
clippings.title: Telescope: A Talk with Hitchcock
clippings.context: Herrmann on CBC Telescope (1964), comparing Hitchcock's screen world to Dickens and the Victorian novelists.

clippings.speaker: Bernard Herrmann
clippings.quote: No, it’s Hitchcock. He just wanted pop stuff, and I said, ‘No, I’m not interested.’ I told him, ‘Hitch, what’s the use of my doing more with you? Your pictures, your mathematics, three zeroes. My mathematics, quite different.’
clippings.title: An Interview with Bernard Herrmann (1911-1975)
clippings.context: Interviewed by Royal S. Brown in New York in August 1975, four months before his death, asked whether the Hitchcock break was the producers' doing; text as revised from the tape for Brown's 1994 book Overtones and Undertones.

clippings.speaker: Bernard Herrmann
clippings.quote: I said, ‘Look, Hitch, you can’t out-jump your own shadow. And you don’t make pop pictures. What do you want with me? I don’t write pop music.’ It’s a mistake, I feel. Because … he only finishes a picture 60 percent. I have to finish it for him.
clippings.title: An Interview with Bernard Herrmann (1911-1975)
clippings.context: Same August 1975 Royal S. Brown interview, on Hitchcock's demand for a pop score for Torn Curtain; source of the oft-repeated '60 percent' line.

clippings.speaker: Bernard Herrmann
clippings.quote: Hitch came to the recording session, listened a while, and said, ‘Look. If I want Herrmann, I’d ask Herrmann. Where’s Mancini?’
clippings.title: An Interview with Bernard Herrmann (1911-1975)
clippings.context: Same 1975 interview: Herrmann recounts how Hitchcock threw out Henry Mancini's Frenzy score (1972) for sounding too much like Herrmann; Hitchcock's words are as relayed by Herrmann.

clippings.speaker: Alfred Hitchcock
clippings.quote: I AM VERY ANXIOUS FOR YOU TO DO THE MUSIC ON TORN CURTAIN STOP … UNFORTUNATELY FOR WE ARTISTS WE DO NOT HAVE THE FREEDOM THAT WE WOULD LIKE TO HAVE BECAUSE WE ARE CATERING TO AN AUDIENCE AND THAT IS WHY YOU GET YOUR MONEY AND I GET MINE STOP
clippings.title: We are catering to an audience and that is why you get your money and I get mine
clippings.context: Hitchcock's telegram to Herrmann ('DEAR BENNY'), 4 November 1965, asking for a modern 'beat' score; reproduced on the Stars and Letters blog from Dan Auiler's Hitchcock's Notebooks (1999).

clippings.speaker: Alfred Hitchcock
clippings.quote: thirty three and a third of Psycho’s success was due to Bernard Herrmann’s music.
clippings.title: Herrmann and Hitchcock – The Torn Curtain
clippings.context: Steve Vertlieb's 2002 Midnight Marquee essay says Hitchcock 'would often proclaim to interviewers' this after Psycho; no original interview is cited, and wording varies elsewhere (e.g. '33% of the effect of Psycho was due to the music').

clippings.speaker: Alfred Hitchcock
clippings.quote: Yes … if he’ll do as he’s told.
clippings.title: Herrmann and Hitchcock – The Torn Curtain
clippings.context: Per Vertlieb (2002), Hitchcock's answer years after the Torn Curtain firing, at a University of Southern California speaking engagement, when asked if he'd ever work with Herrmann again; no date or original source given.

clippings.speaker: Jack Lemmon
clippings.quote: I always like to say that what Billy did so successfully was to grow a rose in a garbage pail, because he told a romance, he made you care about these two people, with their flaws—it’s interesting that both of them are flawed. And he made you care about them. At the same time, he made a hell of a lot of personal comment about our business society and our mores and behavior—and made the best picture of the year.
clippings.title: Jack Lemmon Looks Back on His Seven-Film Partnership with Billy Wilder
clippings.context: From Lally's 1993 phone interview with Lemmon for his Wilder biography Wilder Times (Holt, 1996); the full transcript was first posted on Lally's site in 2022.

clippings.speaker: Jack Lemmon
clippings.quote: I’d pop into the office any time I got an idea, and Billy would think about it and he’d smile a little and he’d say, ‘Wait and show me.’ Whenever I had an idea, he’d always stop me from telling it and say, ‘Don’t tell me. I might misunderstand. No. Show me.’ And he was always wide open.
clippings.title: Jack Lemmon Looks Back on His Seven-Film Partnership with Billy Wilder
clippings.context: Same 1993 Lally interview; Lemmon is answering whether he and Wilder discussed the character of C.C. Baxter before shooting.

clippings.speaker: Jack Lemmon
clippings.quote: I wished that Billy had been a little looser as the writer and let us overlap and charge it more, and screw the lines. But Billy the writer, I know, does not like to have any of his words not heard. … If I have to fault Billy at all, I would fault him on that minor level only.
clippings.title: Jack Lemmon Looks Back on His Seven-Film Partnership with Billy Wilder
clippings.context: Same 1993 Lally interview; Lemmon names The Front Page (1974) as one of his least favorite of their films and gives his one criticism of Wilder.

clippings.speaker: Jack Lemmon
clippings.quote: We (then) went to Billy’s office, and he looked and said, ‘Hello, girls.’ I told him what we just did, and I said, ‘Not one girl batted an eyeball.’ He said, ‘Don’t touch anything.’
clippings.title: In Retrospect: Hollywood Legend Jack Lemmon Looks Back on Making ‘Some Like It Hot’
clippings.context: 1993 interview by Judy Sloane (portions first published in Film Review Magazine); Lemmon and Tony Curtis had just tested their drag looks in the Goldwyn lot's ladies' room.

clippings.speaker: Jack Lemmon
clippings.quote: The best single piece of direction I’ve ever gotten came from Billy Wilder, while we were making ‘Some Like It Hot.’ It’s the scene just after I’ve become engaged to the Joe E. Brown character. … Billy handed me the maracas and said, ‘In your happiness and joy, you dance with these things.’ It was a stroke of genius. It served as both pause and punctuation.
clippings.title: Wilder With a Twist of Lemmon
clippings.context: Paul Freeman's 1994 report on a joint Q&A with Wilder and Lemmon at the Stanford Theatre, Palo Alto; Lemmon was handed a pair of maracas on stage.

clippings.speaker: Billy Wilder
clippings.quote: Nobody's perfect, but he came as close.
clippings.title: Remembering Jack Lemmon
clippings.context: Wilder's statement on Lemmon's death, issued through a spokesman and read on air by Larry King, who also relayed that Wilder was "saddened by the loss of his friend Jack Lemmon, a great actor an a wonderful man."

clippings.speaker: Billy Wilder
clippings.quote: He was a wonderful guy … I loved him dearly and he was the best actor I ever worked with.
clippings.title: Hollywood Remembers Jack Lemmon
clippings.context: Wilder speaking to the Los Angeles Times after Lemmon's death, as quoted in ABC News's roundup of tributes (June 29, 2001); ABC also reports Wilder told Variety's Army Archerd he couldn't pick a favorite of their films: "I choose them all."

clippings.speaker: Billy Wilder
clippings.quote: Jack Lemmon is a ham. And you can always trim a ham. Jack Lemmon always gives you everything.
clippings.title: JACK LEMMON 1925-2001 // Farewell to America's Everyman
clippings.context: Quoted in Lemmon's obituary as something Wilder "once said"; the original occasion is not given.

clippings.speaker: Billy Wilder
clippings.quote: He has his own opinion on things, but he's not bullheaded about it
clippings.title: Behind the Camera - The Apartment
clippings.context: Rob Nixon's TCM production history of The Apartment quotes Wilder on Lemmon's cooperativeness, without naming the original interview.

clippings.speaker: Billy Wilder
clippings.quote: Happiness is working with Jack Lemmon
clippings.title: Duncan Campbell on Jack Lemmon, a 'beautiful actor'
clippings.context: Wilder's much-repeated line, cited in the Guardian's report on Lemmon's death as how Wilder "once described him"; no original source located.
